usage: Used when describing a task or activity that is extremely easy to accomplish.
grammar_pattern: It was/is a piece of cake to + verb
common_mistakes: Trying to use it in formal writing
example_sentences: Passing the driving test was a piece of cake after all those lessons.
Don't worry about the presentation; for someone with your experience, it'll be a piece of cake.
I thought fixing the computer would be hard, but it turned out to be a piece of cake.
To be honest, the exam was a piece of cake.
Is the new software difficult to learn? No, it's a piece of cake.
collocations: seems like a piece of cake
turn out to be a piece of cake
native_notes: Very common in spoken British English. Avoid in IELTS Writing Task 2 as it is an idiom.

usage: Used when you are extremely tired after a long day or intense physical activity.
example_sentences: I've been working since 6 am and I am absolutely knackered.
After that football match, the whole team was knackered.
Are you coming out tonight? No, I'm knackered, I'm just going to sleep.
He looked completely knackered after carrying those boxes upstairs.
I’m knackered, let’s take a break.
native_notes: A quintessential British slang term. Much more expressive than simply saying 'very tired'.

usage: Commonly used by students when they need to start studying intensively for an exam.
example_sentences: I have a massive exam on Monday, so I need to hit the books all weekend.
I can't go to the cinema tonight, I really need to hit the books.
If you don't hit the books now, you'll regret it during finals week.
He’s been hitting the books for hours, he must be exhausted.
It’s time to hit the books if we want to pass this module.
native_notes: Very common among university students. It implies a sense of urgency and focus.

usage: Widely used in the UK as a casual way to say 'thank you' or as a toast when drinking.
common_mistakes: Using it in very formal business emails
Expecting it to mean 'goodbye' in all regions
example_sentences: Cheers for helping me with those heavy bags!
Could you pass the salt? Yes, sure. Cheers.
I'll see you tomorrow then. Cheers!
Cheers to a great year ahead! (while raising a glass)
Thanks for the coffee. Cheers, mate.
native_notes: In the UK, it is the most common casual way to say thanks. It can also serve as a parting word in informal speech.

usage: Used when someone is wasting time instead of being productive, or acting in a silly way.
example_sentences: Stop messing around and get your homework finished.
We spent the whole afternoon messing around at the park instead of studying.
I don't like it when my colleagues mess around during the morning meeting.
He's just messing around with the new phone to see how it works.
If we mess around too long, we’ll miss the last train.
native_notes: Often carries a slightly frustrated tone when directed at someone who should be working.

usage: Used when someone is hesitating to do something new and you want to encourage them to try.
alternatives: to have a crack at it
to have a shot at it
example_sentences: I’ve never played tennis before, but I’ll give it a go.
You should apply for the job; why not give it a go?
It looks difficult, but I’m going to give it a go.
Just give it a go, the worst that can happen is you fail.
Thanks for the suggestion, I think I’ll give it a go.
collocations: willing to give it a go
native_notes: This implies a casual, low-stakes attempt. It suggests a positive, open-minded attitude towards a challenge.

usage: Used to describe a task or activity that is incredibly easy to complete.
grammar_pattern: Subject + be + a piece of cake
common_mistakes: using it to describe a person
example_sentences: The driving test was a piece of cake.
Don't worry about the presentation, it'll be a piece of cake.
For a professional chef, cooking dinner for four is a piece of cake.
I thought the maths exam would be hard, but it was a piece of cake.
Fixing the computer settings was a piece of cake.
collocations: turned out to be a piece of cake
thought it would be a piece of cake
native_notes: A classic idiom. It is widely understood but avoid overusing it in IELTS Speaking as it has become a bit of a cliché.

usage: Used to describe spending time with friends in a relaxed, unstructured way.
example_sentences: I usually hang out with my cousins at the weekend.
Do you want to come over and hang out tonight?
We spent the whole afternoon just hanging out at the park.
It’s great to hang out with friends after a stressful week.
Where do you usually hang out in this city?
native_notes: Essential for everyday social English. It implies no specific plan or agenda, just enjoying company.

usage: Used to express deep disappointment or sadness about a specific event or news.
example_sentences: I was absolutely gutted when I heard the news about the concert being cancelled.
She was gutted to miss her best friend’s wedding.
We were all gutted that we lost the game in the final minute.
Don’t be gutted, there will be plenty more opportunities.
I’m gutted I can’t make it to your party tonight.
native_notes: Very common British slang. It captures a stronger feeling than just 'disappointed'.

usage: Used when finishing a meeting, a project, or a task.
grammar_pattern: Wrap + object + up / Wrap up + object
example_sentences: Right, let's wrap this meeting up so we can all go home.
We need to wrap up the project by Friday afternoon.
Can we wrap this conversation up later? I'm in a rush.
The director decided to wrap up filming early due to the bad weather.
It's about time we wrapped things up for the day.
native_notes: Very versatile. Can be used for physical tasks (wrapping a gift) or abstract ones (a business project).

expression: to be a piece of cake
usage: Used to describe a task that is extremely easy to complete.
grammar_pattern: Subject + be + a piece of cake
common_mistakes: The exam was like a piece of cake
example_sentences: Don't worry about the driving test, it'll be a piece of cake for you.
I thought the computer repair would be difficult, but it was a piece of cake.
Learning the basics of the language was a piece of cake.
For a professional like her, that project is a piece of cake.
Setting up the new account turned out to be a piece of cake.
collocations: it was a piece of cake
thought it would be a piece of cake
native_notes: Very idiomatic. Sounds natural in Speaking Part 1 and 2, but avoid in academic writing.

usage: Used when you decide to relax and let things happen naturally instead of trying to control them.
alternatives: to take things as they come
example_sentences: I don't have a fixed plan for the holiday; I think I'll just go with the flow.
When you're travelling, it's best to just go with the flow if things don't go as planned.
She’s a very relaxed person who prefers to go with the flow.
We didn't have an agenda, so we just went with the flow.
I’m happy to go with the flow regarding the restaurant choice.
collocations: prefer to go with the flow
learn to go with the flow
native_notes: Conveys a sense of maturity and lack of stress regarding uncertainty.

uzbek: qo'ldan boy bermoq, imkoniyatni o'tkazib yubormoq
usage: Used when someone does not get the benefit or enjoyment of something, often due to an oversight.
alternatives: to fail to take advantage of
example_sentences: If you don't book the tickets soon, you'll miss out on the concert.
I stayed in all weekend and felt like I was missing out on the fun.
He didn't want to miss out on the chance to study abroad.
Many students miss out on networking opportunities by not attending events.
Don't miss out on our special offer ending tonight!
native_notes: The 'on' is essential. It is frequently used to express a sense of regret or lost potential.

usage: Used to ask someone to wait for a moment or to express slight surprise/disbelief.
grammar_pattern: Hang on + (imperative) / Hang on a minute + clause
common_mistakes: using it in a formal workplace email
example_sentences: Hang on, I think I left my keys in the car.
Hang on a minute, did you say the meeting is tomorrow?
Could you hang on while I grab my coat?
Hang on, let me check the schedule before we decide.
Hang on, that doesn't sound right to me.
native_notes: Very versatile. It can be used to stop someone from speaking, to buy time, or to signal that you need to rethink a previous statement.

usage: Used when you decide to stop doing something, usually work or study, for the remainder of the day because you are tired or finished.
grammar_pattern: Let's call it a day / We decided to call it a day
example_sentences: We've been working for ten hours; let's call it a day.
It's getting quite late, so we should probably call it a day.
I'm exhausted, so I think I'll call it a day and go home.
Since we've finished the main task, let's call it a day.
They decided to call it a day after failing to reach a compromise.
collocations: decide to call it a day
time to call it a day
ready to call it a day
native_notes: Essential for work-life balance conversations. It implies a voluntary decision to stop rather than an external constraint.

uzbek: boshim aylanib ketyapti / garang bo'lib qoldim
usage: Used when you are confused, overwhelmed by too much information, or experiencing vertigo.
grammar_pattern: My head is spinning from + noun/V-ing
common_mistakes: using it to describe being angry
example_sentences: There's so much information in this module that my head is spinning.
My head is spinning from all the different instructions you gave me.
After listening to the complex physics lecture, my head was spinning.
My head is spinning; I need to take a break from this screen.
Trying to learn three languages at once has left my head spinning.
native_notes: Can be literal (medical) or metaphorical (cognitive overload). Context usually makes it clear which one is meant.
russian: У меня кружится голова / кружится голова

usage: Used when you decide to try doing something, especially something new or difficult.
grammar_pattern: Give it a go / Give + [activity] + a go
example_sentences: I'm not sure if I can fix the sink, but I'll give it a go.
Why don't you give it a go and see how you like it?
It looks challenging, but I'm willing to give it a go.
I was nervous about public speaking, but I decided to give it a go.
If you've never tried surfing before, just give it a go!
collocations: willing to give it a go
decide to give it a go
ready to give it a go
native_notes: Very common British English idiom. It sounds slightly more enthusiastic and proactive than just saying 'try'.

usage: Used to describe a relaxed person or a calm atmosphere.
common_mistakes: Using 'chilling out' to describe a person's character
example_sentences: My boss is quite chilled out, so we don't feel much pressure at work.
We spent a chilled out weekend watching films and catching up on sleep.
I love hanging out in this cafe; it's such a chilled out place.
You need to be a bit more chilled out about the results.
After the exam, we had a chilled out evening in the park.
native_notes: Differs from 'chill out' (the phrasal verb meaning to relax). 'Chilled out' (adjective) describes a state or a personality trait.

usage: Used when meeting someone after a long time to exchange news or updates.
common_mistakes: Saying 'catch with' instead of 'catch up with'
Using 'catch up' when you just met yesterday
example_sentences: It was lovely to catch up with my old university friends over coffee.
We have so much to catch up on since we haven't spoken in months.
Let's meet for lunch next week to catch up.
I had a long phone call with my mum just to catch up on family news.
It's impossible to catch up on everything in just one short meeting.
native_notes: Can also mean 'to do work you missed' (e.g., catching up on emails), but in social contexts, it always implies updating each other on life events.
russian: поболтать (поговорить о новостях, которые вы пропустили)

usage: Used to describe someone doing more than is required to achieve a goal or please someone.
common_mistakes: Using 'do the extra mile' instead of 'go'
example_sentences: Our teacher always goes the extra mile to help students with their applications.
If you want to get a Band 8, you really have to go the extra mile.
The hotel staff went the extra mile to make our anniversary special.
She is a dedicated employee who always goes the extra mile for her clients.
I was impressed that they went the extra mile to fix the issue so quickly.
collocations: willing to go the extra mile
go the extra mile for someone
go the extra mile to do something
ready to go the extra mile
native_notes: Widely used in both business settings and general conversation to praise dedication.

usage: Used when you are annoyed or bored because a situation has continued for too long.
grammar_pattern: Subject + be + fed up with + noun/gerund
common_mistakes: Using 'fed up of' instead of 'fed up with'
alternatives: At the end of my tether
example_sentences: I'm fed up with this constant rainy weather.
He got fed up with waiting for the bus, so he decided to walk.
Are you fed up with your current job yet?
I am completely fed up with people talking during the film.
After three hours of delays, everyone was fed up with the airline.
native_notes: Use 'with' rather than 'of'. 'Fed up of' is commonly heard but technically non-standard in British English.

usage: Used to say you are starting a task or continuing with a task energetically.
common_mistakes: thinking it means to break something
example_sentences: We've got a lot to finish, so let's crack on.
I need to crack on with my essay if I want to finish by tonight.
Stop chatting and crack on with your homework!
It's getting late, I better crack on with the laundry.
Once we finish lunch, we should crack on with the project.
native_notes: It carries a sense of urgency and focus. It is very idiomatic and sounds natural in a working or study context.
russian: продолжить работу, начать как можно скорее

uzbek: o'zini baxtiyor his qilmoq, yetti osmonda bo'lmoq
usage: Used when expressing extreme happiness about an event or news.
common_mistakes: saying 'on the moon' instead of 'over the moon'
using it for small, unimportant things
example_sentences: I was over the moon when I got the acceptance letter.
She's over the moon with her new job offer.
They are over the moon about the birth of their baby.
I was over the moon when I passed my IELTS with a band 8.
He's over the moon to have won the competition.
native_notes: A very popular idiom that adds colour and emotion to an IELTS speaking answer.
russian: чувствовать себя счастливым, быть на небесах

usage: Used when you think someone is teasing you or telling you a lie for fun.
common_mistakes: Taking it literally as a physical action
example_sentences: Wait, did you really win the lottery, or are you just pulling my leg?
He told me he met a celebrity, but I knew he was pulling my leg.
Stop pulling my leg! There is no way that happened.
I wasn't sure if she was serious or just pulling my leg.
It's hard to tell when he's pulling my leg because he stays so serious.
native_notes: A quintessential British idiom. It implies a lighthearted, harmless deception.

uzbek: o'zini yo'qotib qo'ymoq, aqldan ozmoq, vaziyatni boshqara olmaslik
usage: Used when someone starts acting strangely, becomes angry, or loses their ability to behave logically or calmly.
common_mistakes: Saying 'lost my plot' instead of 'lost the plot'
Using it to mean 'lost my place in a story'
example_sentences: He completely lost the plot when he found out the train was cancelled.
I think the manager has lost the plot; he's making no sense lately.
When the pressure mounted, she just lost the plot and started shouting.
I hope I don't lose the plot during my presentation tomorrow.
The project is a disaster because the supervisor has totally lost the plot.
native_notes: Very British. 'Losing the plot' often suggests losing one's grip on a situation or logic.
russian: потерять себя, потерять рассудок, оказаться не в состоянии контролировать ситуацию

usage: Used to describe spending relaxed, unstructured time with friends or in a specific place.
grammar_pattern: hang out + with + person / in + place
example_sentences: We usually hang out at the local coffee shop after class.
I love hanging out with my cousins during the summer holidays.
Do you want to hang out this weekend?
Most of the teenagers hang out by the skate park.
It's just a place to hang out and relax.
native_notes: Very common among younger generations. Informal, so never use in formal letters or essays.

usage: British slang for leaving a place quickly, often to avoid paying for something or to avoid an unpleasant situation.
common_mistakes: Using it to mean going for a jog
example_sentences: The kids did a runner as soon as they saw the teacher coming.
The customer tried to do a runner without paying the bill.
When the police arrived, the suspects did a runner.
I hate these awkward parties; I usually do a runner after an hour.
He did a runner the moment things got too serious.
native_notes: This is very British-focused. It carries a slightly cheeky or rebellious tone.

usage: Used when leaving a place briefly to go somewhere close, like a shop or a neighbour's house.
common_mistakes: saying 'I pop out to work' (implies you are leaving forever/not coming back soon)
alternatives: to step out for a moment
example_sentences: I’m just going to pop out to the shops for some milk.
Could you watch the house while I pop out to see my neighbour?
He popped out for a cigarette and hasn't returned yet.
I’ll pop out and grab us some lunch, back in ten minutes.
She popped out to the post office and should be back any second.
native_notes: Suggests a short, casual departure. 'Nip out' is a very similar British regional variation.

usage: Used to relax or to tell someone to calm down.
common_mistakes: using 'chill' to replace all instances of relax
example_sentences: I’m just going to chill out on the sofa and watch some TV.
After a stressful exam, you need to chill out for a few days.
Hey, chill out! It’s not the end of the world.
We usually chill out in the park on Sunday afternoons.
If you’re feeling anxious, try to chill out with some music.
native_notes: Very versatile. Can mean 'do nothing' or 'calm your emotions'. Used heavily by younger generations.

expression: to get the hang of something
uzbek: biror narsani o'rganib olmoq / tushunib qolmoq
usage: Used when you finally learn how to do something that previously seemed difficult or confusing.
grammar_pattern: Subject + get + the hang of + noun/gerund
common_mistakes: get the hang for it (must be 'of')
example_sentences: At first, coding was hard, but I’m starting to get the hang of it.
It took a while to get the hang of driving a manual car.
Don't worry if you're struggling; you'll get the hang of it soon enough.
I've finally got the hang of using this new software for work.
Does your daughter have the hang of playing the guitar yet?
collocations: starting to get the hang of
native_notes: Implies a process of trial and error before reaching success.

usage: Used when you decide to stop working on something for the rest of the day, usually because you are tired or finished.
example_sentences: We've been at the office for ten hours; let's call it a day.
The project is almost done, but I think we should call it a day and finish tomorrow.
It's getting late, shall we call it a day?
I think we've accomplished enough for now, let's call it a day.
After four hours of studying, I decided to call it a day.
collocations: think we should call it a day
time to call it a day
decide to call it a day
native_notes: Very idiomatic; used frequently in work and student environments.

uzbek: biror narsani o'rganib qolmoq, qo'li kelishib qolmoq
usage: Used when you are starting to understand or become proficient at a new skill after some practice.
grammar_pattern: get the hang of + something/doing something
example_sentences: It took me a few days, but I'm finally getting the hang of this software.
Don't worry if you're struggling; you'll get the hang of it eventually.
I’m still getting the hang of driving on the left side of the road.
She got the hang of the new workout routine really quickly.
I thought I’d never understand tennis, but I’m starting to get the hang of it.
collocations: starting to get the hang of
hard to get the hang of
slow to get the hang of
native_notes: This implies a process. It suggests you were bad at it initially but are now improving.

uzbek: o'zini yomon his qilmoq (kasalman degan ma'noda)
usage: Used when you feel slightly ill, but not necessarily seriously sick.
common_mistakes: Using it for serious illnesses like cancer (too informal and trivializing)
example_sentences: I'm feeling a bit under the weather today, so I think I'll stay home.
He's been under the weather all week with a nasty cold.
She decided to miss the party because she was feeling under the weather.
If you're feeling under the weather, you should probably get some rest.
I didn't want to go out while I was feeling under the weather.
collocations: feeling a bit under the weather
look a bit under the weather
native_notes: This is a polite/soft way to tell a boss or friend you aren't feeling well. Avoid using it for life-threatening or serious medical conditions.
russian: чувствовать себя плохо (в смысле быть больным)

usage: Used to show that you accept an excuse or a point of view, even if it is not what you initially wanted.
common_mistakes: It is fair enough (usually used as an interjection)
alternatives: I get where you're coming from
example_sentences: I can't go to the cinema tonight because I'm broke. - Fair enough.
He said he was too busy to help, so fair enough.
I understand why you're upset. Fair enough, I'll apologise.
You want to change the schedule? Fair enough, let's do it.
I don't like horror movies. - Fair enough, let's pick a comedy.
native_notes: Extremely common way to end a debate or disagreement without being aggressive. It shows maturity in conversation.

usage: A very British way of saying you are pleased or proud about something.
grammar_pattern: Subject + be + chuffed + (to V / with N)
example_sentences: I was really chuffed with my exam results.
She was chuffed to bits when she heard the news.
I'm well chuffed that you could make it.
He's chuffed with his new car.
I'm chuffed for you; that's fantastic news!
native_notes: Mainly British English. Use 'well chuffed' for emphasis. 'Chuffed to bits' is a classic idiomatic intensifier.

usage: Used when someone leaves quickly, often to avoid paying for something or to escape a difficult situation.
example_sentences: The customer did a runner before paying the bill.
As soon as the teacher started asking questions, he did a runner.
I saw them do a runner when the police car turned the corner.
Don't try to do a runner; we need to finish this meeting.
He did a runner because he didn't want to help clean up.
native_notes: Has a slightly humorous or mischievous tone. Not necessarily criminal, but definitely avoiding a social or financial obligation.

usage: Idiomatic way to describe heavy rainfall.
common_mistakes: Using it to describe light rain
example_sentences: I forgot my umbrella and it's been raining buckets since I left the house.
Look outside, it’s coming down in buckets!
We had to cancel the picnic because it was raining buckets all afternoon.
Even though it was raining buckets, the football match continued.
It's forecast to rain buckets tomorrow, so don't plan anything outdoors.
native_notes: More natural than the cliché 'raining cats and dogs', which is rarely used by modern native speakers.

expression: to be a bit of a nightmare
usage: Used to describe a situation, journey, or task that is frustrating, difficult, or chaotic.
grammar_pattern: It + be + a bit of a nightmare + (for/to + verb)
common_mistakes: using it to describe a person (unless being quite rude)
example_sentences: The traffic on the motorway was a bit of a nightmare this morning.
Trying to get all the documents ready was a bit of a nightmare.
Moving house is always a bit of a nightmare, isn't it?
The software update was a bit of a nightmare to install.
I'm sorry I'm late; getting a taxi was a bit of a nightmare.
native_notes: The phrase 'a bit of a' acts as a softener, making the complaint sound more conversational and less aggressive.
